120.title: Om jai jagadish hare
120.carry: victory to the lord of the world
120.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and temples, especially in North India and the diaspora, Om jai jagadish hare is sung while the arti lamp is circled at the end of puja, with a bell ringing and everyone joining in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, camphor, the flame that burns bright and leaves no ash, circled clockwise. Your line was light, circled.

A housewarming. The living room is packed, shoes piled by the door. Someone lights the lamp, someone rings a bell, and an aunt starts a tune. By the second line the room has joined in. Grandparents sing it loudly. Teenagers half-sing it. You could hear the same tune at a Diwali party, or on a Sunday evening at a temple in Houston or Leicester or Nairobi. Yesterday you circled the flame. This is the song that often goes with it.
screen: `A PACKED ROOM, ONE TUNE.` → `LIVING ROOMS AND TEMPLES.` → `TODAY: THE ARTI SONG.`

segments.voice: The song is Om jai jagadish hare. It isn't ancient. It's usually credited to Shardha Ram Phillauri, a Punjabi writer of the eighteen-hundreds, and it's in Hindi, not Sanskrit. Some say that's part of why it spread: anyone could understand it. Here's the first line, the one everybody knows: Om jai jagadish hare, swami jai jagadish hare. Word by word: Om, the first sound, your word from day two. Jai, victory, or glory, the word people shout at festivals. Jagadish is two words joined: jagat, the world, the moving universe, and ish, lord. The lord of the world. Hare calls on Hari, a name of Vishnu that tradition explains as the one who takes away. Swami means master, lord. So: Om, victory to you, lord of the world, O Hari. Victory, master, to the lord of the world. Then the verse says why: the troubles of your devotees, of those who serve you, you take away in a moment. That's the whole song in small. It isn't a request list. It starts with praise, jai, and only then remembers that people are hurting, and trusts that help comes quickly. It's addressed to Vishnu, but it's often sung at the end of other pujas too, to whatever form is on the shelf. And it's sung while the flame circles: the tune and the light move together.
screen: `NOT ANCIENT, AND IN HINDI.` · `JAI — VICTORY, GLORY.` · `JAGAT + ISH: LORD OF THE WORLD.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN THE TROUBLES.`

segments.voice: Slowly, and even if singing isn't your thing, speak it, sing it or just listen inside: Om jai jagadish hare, swami jai jagadish hare. Once more, a little slower, and if you'd like, let your flame or your open hand circle with the tune. Then let the sound stop and sit in what's left of it; if you don't pray, simply listen to the words and the tune.
Hari, a name of Vishnu, the one who takes away: called on in the arti song, Om Jai Jagadish Hare, victory to you, lord of the world. Today's word.
Your line: victory to the lord of the world. Praise first, and only then the troubles. Day one hundred twenty, done.

121.title: Taking the light
121.howItsDone: At the end of arti, the lamp is brought to each person, who passes cupped hands over the flame without touching it and then touches the hands to the eyes, face or head; in temples, people often place a small offering on the plate as it passes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hari, called on in the arti song, Om jai jagadish hare. Your line was victory to the lord of the world.
screen: `OM JAI JAGADISH HARE — VICTORY TO THE LORD OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Your first arti with a Hindu friend, and there's a moment that can catch you off guard. The song ends. The bell stops. Then the person holding the lamp turns around and walks toward you, holding out the plate with the flame still burning. Everyone near you does something with their hands, quickly, easily, like they've done it all their lives. And you stand there wondering: am I supposed to touch it? Blow on it? Pass?
screen: `THE SONG ENDS.` → `THE PLATE COMES TOWARD YOU.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH YOUR HANDS?`

segments.voice: Here's what people are doing. When the arti plate reaches you, you cup your hands and pass them over the flame, close enough to feel the warmth, never touching. Then you draw your hands back and bring them to your eyes, your face, sometimes over the top of your head. Some do it twice or three times. Some use both hands, some only the right. It takes about three seconds. Why? The flame has just been circled before the divine. It has been, you might say, in the presence. Now it comes out to the people, and you take a little of that light and warmth into yourself: over the eyes, so you see well; over the head, as a blessing. Remember your fourteenth word, arti, and its line, light passed hand to hand. This is that line, literally: the light went to the shrine, and now it goes from palm to palm through the whole room. A few quiet customs travel with it. An arti flame usually isn't blown out; blowing on a sacred flame is often seen as disrespectful, so it's left to burn down or put out another way. In temples, people often drop a coin or a small note on the plate as it passes. And if you're a guest and unsure, it's fine to watch first, then copy the person next to you. Nobody is keeping score. The light is offered to everyone in the room.
screen: `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, NOT TOUCHING.` · `BACK TO THE EYES, THE FACE, THE HEAD.` · `LIGHT PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `DON'T BLOW IT OUT.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or lamp and it's safe, light it and set it steady in front of you; if not, picture the arti plate coming toward you. Cup your hands and pass them slowly over the warmth, a few inches above, never touching, then draw them back and rest your palms softly over your closed eyes, feeling the warmth there. Once more, and this time let your hands pass over the top of your head, then rest them in your lap and stay with the flame.
Jyoti, the flame: after arti, hands pass over it and come back to the eyes and the head, taking the shrine's light into yourself. Today's word.
Your line: take it. Three seconds: hands over the flame, then back to your eyes. Until tomorrow.

122.title: Family arti
122.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes, evening arti is a family gathering: one person circles the lamp, a child often rings the bell, everyone sings, and the lamp is passed around so each person can take the light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jyoti, the flame: hands passed over it, then to the eyes. Your line was take it.

Evening arti in a childhood home. Dad holding the plate a little too high. A little sister fighting to ring the bell, and ringing it the entire time. An aunt singing half a beat ahead of everyone. The smell of camphor, and dinner waiting in the next room. For ten minutes, the whole house was facing the same way. Years later, what stays often isn't the words. It's who was there. The hour, the flame, the song, the light: all of it works alone. But arti was built for more than one.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE REMEMBER: WHO WAS THERE.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE FACING ONE WAY.` → `TODAY: FAMILY ARTI.`

segments.voice: Look at how arti is put together and you'll see it almost asks for company. It has jobs. Someone holds the lamp. Someone rings the bell, often the youngest, because it's the best job. Everyone sings. Then the plate goes around, and each person takes the light. Even the smallest child has something to do. Hindu tradition names four stages of life, and the second, the householder, grihastha, is the one lived in a home full of people. The Manusmriti calls it the stage that supports the others, the way air supports every living thing, because the householder feeds and gives to all the rest. And the home shrine sits right in the middle of it. Worship isn't something you leave the house to do; the house is where it's done. So evening arti becomes a kind of daily meeting. The day's arguments get paused. The phones go down, or at least face down. For ten minutes, whoever is under that roof stands together before one flame. Real families are complicated, though. Some people live alone. Some live with a partner from another faith, or with none. Nobody is saying anyone has to join; a guest can simply stand in the room, listen and watch. But the invitation matters. Prayer can happen alone, anywhere. Arti done together adds something else: the same small flame passing through every pair of hands under one roof.
screen: `ARTI HAS JOBS: LAMP, BELL, SONG.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER: GRIHASTHA.` · `THE HOUSE IS WHERE IT'S DONE.` · `NO ONE HAS TO. EVERYONE IS ASKED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you could invite to do this with you, even once: a roommate, a parent on a video call, a partner, a child, a friend. Picture them in the room, one of you holding the flame and one ringing the bell, and notice how it feels not to be the only one facing the light. Then think how you might ask them, simply, with no pressure at all; if they say no, that's fine too.
Family arti. Arti done together: one lamp, one bell, one song, and a job for everyone in the house. Today's word.
Your line: one more. No one has to join, and everyone can be asked. That's day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: Sunset without objects
123.hook: arti with nothing but the actual sun
123.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the sun directly, pouring water toward it at dawn or bowing to it at the twilight junctions; when no shrine is available, some simply face the rising or setting sun with folded hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, family arti: a job for everyone in the house. Your line was one more.

You're in a hospital waiting room. Or an airport. Or a dorm where candles are banned, or a friend's house, or a work trip in a hotel with a window that doesn't open. No shelf, no lamp, no bell, no flower. It's evening, and this week's arti has nowhere to happen. Take away every object from this week, the lamp, the plate, the camphor, the song sheet. What's left? One answer is right there. Look out the window.
screen: `NO SHELF, NO LAMP, NO BELL.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?` → `LOOK OUT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Long before there were brass lamps and printed arti songs, there were the Vedas. The very first hymn of the Rig Veda is to Agni, fire, praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who carries offerings to the gods. Other hymns sing to the dawn, and to the sun. The Gayatri, from day one hundred eight, asks the light of the sun to wake up the mind. The sun has a special title in Hindu tradition: it's sometimes called the god you can actually see. You don't need an image to imagine it; it's right there every day, rising and setting. Here's one way to see the arti lamp. Every evening, as the sun goes down, a household lights a small flame and holds it up. The little flame is a kind of stand-in for the big one, carried indoors for the night. The sun is the original flame, so when you have nothing, you still have it. On day one hundred fifteen, water was poured toward the sun at dawn. At dusk, you can simply turn west, where the sun is setting, put your hands together, and watch: the light that crossed the sky all day, finishing its path in front of you. One practical thing. Never stare straight into the sun. Watch the sky around it, the colors, the edges of the clouds. The light will find your face without your help.
screen: `THE RIG VEDA OPENS WITH FIRE.` · `THE GOD YOU CAN ACTUALLY SEE.` · `THE LAMP IS A STAND-IN.` · `FACE WEST. HANDS TOGETHER. WATCH.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn toward the west, toward a window or where the sun sets even if it's hidden right now; if it's not evening, picture the last sunset you remember well. Put your hands together at your chest if you'd like, and look at the sky around the sun, never at the sun itself. Let the color be the flame and the whole horizon the plate: nothing to hold, nothing to light, just the original flame and you in front of it.
Surya, the sun, honored as the god you can see: arti with nothing but him, facing west, hands together, watching the original flame go down. Today's word.
Your line: the original flame. Wherever you are, the sun still sets, and no objects are needed. Day one hundred twenty-three, done.

124.title: Your evening routine
124.hook: assemble: bell, breath, arti, one line
124.howItsDone: Many Hindu households close the day with evening arti at the home shrine, often with a bell, the circled lamp, a song or mantra, and a closing invocation of peace such as Om shanti shanti shanti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surya, the sun: just him, and you facing it. Your line was the original flame.

The phone falls on your face at midnight. Most days don't end. They just stop. Last week you built a morning. This week you've gathered the other end of the day, piece by piece. Sandhya, the hour where day and night join. Arti at home, a small flame circled. Om jai jagadish hare, the song everyone knows. Taking the light, hands over the flame to your eyes. Family arti, one more person in the room. And yesterday, the sun itself. Today they become the other bookend: your evening routine.
screen: `MOST DAYS DON'T END, THEY STOP.` → `A WEEK OF DUSK.` → `TODAY: THE OTHER BOOKEND.`

segments.voice: Here's a shape: four pieces, about five minutes, built only from things you already know. First, the bell. One ring, followed all the way to silence: arriving, from day one hundred fourteen. Second, the breath you learned back in week fifteen: in for four, out for six. A few rounds of the longer out-breath tell the body the day is closing. Third, arti. If you have a lamp, light it and circle it slowly, maybe humming the first line of the song. If you don't, face the window, toward where the sun went down. Then take the light: hands over the flame, back to your eyes. And fourth, one line. Many Hindu prayers close the same way, with Om and three shantis: Om shanti, shanti, shanti. Your fourth word, peace, peace, peace. Some people use their own mantra here instead. Just one line, said slowly, as the last thing. Bell, breath, arti, one line. Now notice what it's for. The morning puja offers the day before it starts. The evening routine hands the day back. Whatever happened, the good meeting, the argument, the thing you forgot, you don't have to carry it into sleep. People in many traditions have a way of closing the day. This is one Hindu way: a flame, a breath, a word of peace, and the day put down.
screen: `THE BELL: ARRIVE.` · `THE BREATH: LONGER OUT.` · `ARTI: THE FLAME, OR THE WINDOW.` · `ONE LINE: OM SHANTI, SHANTI, SHANTI.`

segments.voice: Ring your bell or tap a glass and follow the sound to silence, then breathe in for four and out for six, three times. If you have a flame, circle it slowly clockwise and take the light to your eyes, or if not, turn toward the window; then, quietly, if you'd like: Om shanti, shanti, shanti. Last, name one thing from today, just one, and set it down.
Dinacharya, the course of the day: bell, breath, arti, one line, five minutes that close it instead of letting it just stop. Today's word.
Your line: the day put down. Even a shortened version of the four pieces closes it. That's the week, and day one hundred twenty-four.

125.title: The body as temple
125.howItsDone: Many Hindus bathe before morning puja and treat bodily care, food, rest and movement as part of religious life, drawing on the idea, found in later Upanishads and in devotional poetry, that the body is a temple in which the divine dwells.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dinacharya, your evening routine: bell, breath, arti, one line. Your line was the day put down.
screen: `YOUR EVENING ROUTINE — THE DAY PUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: For two weeks you've been building a shrine. A corner, a shelf, a lamp, a flower, a bell, a cup of water. You've learned to keep it clean, bring fresh flowers, light it at the edges of the day. Now look down. At your hands. Your feet. The chest going up and down. There's a shrine you've carried this whole time, one you didn't have to buy, and it's easy to treat it worse than the shelf. Meals get skipped, sleep gets cut, and it only gets noticed when it hurts. This week turns to the body and food. Today: the body as temple.
screen: `TWO WEEKS BUILDING A SHRINE.` → `NOW LOOK DOWN.` → `TODAY: THE BODY AS TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: A short line in the Maitreya Upanishad says it straight out: the body is called a temple, and the living one inside it is Shiva himself. The body is the building. What lives in it is holy. You met that idea on day ten, atman: someone is in there. Today asks what that means for the building. Basavanna, a poet-saint of Karnataka who wrote in Kannada, put it in a poem that's still sung. The rich, he says, build temples for Shiva. What can a poor man do? Then he answers: my legs are the pillars, my body is the shrine, my head is the golden dome. He didn't need stone. He was already standing in one. So looking after the body isn't vanity, and it isn't a chore separate from the spiritual life. Bathing before puja, eating with some care, sleeping enough, moving, resting: these become part of the practice, the way sweeping the shrine is part of puja. And notice what the idea doesn't say. The temple doesn't have to be perfect, young or strong. It can be old, cracked, patched, or hard to climb the steps of. Bodies that are sick, tired, disabled or aging are still temples, and still lived in. The point is who lives there. This week is about caring for the building.
screen: `THE BODY IS CALLED A TEMPLE.` · `BASAVANNA: MY LEGS ARE THE PILLARS.` · `CARE IS PART OF THE PRACTICE.` · `A TEMPLE CAN BE OLD, OR CRACKED.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever's kinder today, and close your eyes if you like. Walk slowly through the temple: your feet, the foundation; the legs, Basavanna's pillars; the belly and chest, moving with the breath; the hands, which did so much work today; the shoulders, where the day usually hides; the face; the top of the head, the dome. Don't fix anything, just visit each part: this is where you live.
Devalaya, a house of God: the old idea that the body itself is this shrine, with someone holy living in it, so caring for it is part of the practice. Today's word.
Your line: this is where you live. A cracked temple is still lived in. See you tomorrow.

126.title: Sun salutation, plainly
126.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice surya namaskar in the morning, facing east, as both exercise and devotion, sometimes reciting one of the twelve names of the sun, such as Om Mitraya namah, with each round.

segments.voice: Yesterday, devalaya: the body as a temple. Your line was this is where you live.
screen: `THE BODY AS TEMPLE — THIS IS WHERE YOU LIVE.`

segments.voice: Arms up. Fold forward. Step back. Down, up, dog, forward, rise. If you've ever taken a yoga class, you've probably done it. The instructor calls it a sun salutation, the music is soft, and everyone is mostly worried about their hamstrings. Nobody mentions the sun. But the name is telling you something. It isn't called the stretch sequence. It's a salutation, a greeting, addressed to someone. Yesterday you walked slowly through the temple of the body. Today you move it, and point it at the original flame from day one hundred and twenty-three.
screen: `ARMS UP, FOLD, STEP BACK.` → `NOBODY MENTIONS THE SUN.` → `A GREETING, TO SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Surya is the sun, the god you can actually see. Namaskar is a bow, from the same root as namaste, your very first word. So: a bow to the sun. In its common form it's a flowing loop of about twelve positions. Stand with palms together. Reach up. Fold forward. Step one leg back into a lunge. Come into a plank, lower down, lift the chest. Push back into a mountain shape, step forward, fold, reach up, and return to standing, palms together. Each movement goes with a breath: in as you open, out as you fold. People who practice it as devotion often add what the gym leaves out: one of the twelve names of the sun, said with each round. The first is Om Mitraya namah: a bow to Mitra, the friend. Now, plainly, the history. Honoring the sun goes back to the Vedic hymns, and bowing to it at dawn is old too. But the exact flowing sequence taught in classes around the world was shaped and made popular quite recently, in the early twentieth century, by a raja in western India who promoted it for health. It's an old devotion wearing a fairly new shape. So it can be two things at once: exercise, and a bow. Some Hindus do it each morning, facing east, as both. What makes it a salutation is the direction you face, and who you have in mind.
